name: PT Mitrabahtera Segara Sejati Tbk

frontmatter.title: Mitrabahtera Segara Sejati: a real coal contract with a finite term
frontmatter.summary: MBSS has re-rated on a change of control and a five-year GEL coal-transport contract. The contract is genuine, but it needs a fleet build that keeps free cash flow negative through FY2028 and it expires in 2031 with no renewal disclosed; the balance sheet is mostly cash and related-party loans. We rate SELL: the operating business does not justify the price.
thesis: The GEL Group contract is a genuine step change - 6.0 Mt a year for five years [S3] - but it is a volume plan, not a take-or-pay revenue line, and serving it consumes cash: MBSS spent IDR372.8bn on vessels in H1-2026 alone [S5].

The last actual year is not a trailing-year benchmark: FY2025A EBITDA of IDR269.4bn is 32.0% of revenue, while H1-2026 earned IDR91.4bn gross profit and an EBITDA margin near a fifth [S5, S6]; the 'LTM' the old multiple used was FY2025A, not the trailing figure.

The balance sheet is the value anchor and the governance risk at once: IDR975.0bn of long-term loans sit with the former controlling shareholder and its affiliates at 8.5% [S6, F13-F15], beside IDR2,143.7bn of cash at 30 June 2026.

The acquisition and the mandatory tender offer both cleared at about Rp2,915/share, leaving the new controller with 90.1% [S7, S8]; the public float is near the exchange minimum, and the company is buying back stock at a price well above our value.
Our DCF values the operating business at IDR843.7bn of enterprise value; net cash and the related-party receivable at face give a twelve-month target of Rp2,613, a -36.7% return - SELL.

blocks.text: We rate MBSS **SELL** with a twelve-month target of Rp2,613, a total return of -36.7% from the Rp4,130 price, with no dividend. The shares have roughly tripled over the past year: an 82.5% stake changed hands at Rp2,915/share in July 2026 [S7], the mandatory tender offer cleared at the same price in October and left Wibowo Group Capital with 90.1% [S8], and on 26 October the company announced a five-year coal-transport contract with GEL Group for 500,000 t/month, 6.0 Mt a year, with potential revenue of IDR1,200.0bn a year [S3]. The market now pays 35.1x FY2026E EV/EBITDA for a business that earned IDR176.2bn of forecast EBITDA [S0].

The variant view is not that the contract is fake. It is that the price treats a volume plan as contracted cash flow while the accounting shows the opposite of a cash business: H1-2026 revenue fell [S5], charter-in costs rose [S5], and the company is spending more on vessels than it earns [S5, F31]. We value the enterprise on free cash flow to the firm, not on the story: the DCF puts enterprise value at IDR843.7bn, with 80.1% of that value in the terminal year; the June-2026 cash of IDR2,143.7bn net of IDR530.6bn of bank loans and IDR4.0bn plus IDR2.1bn of lease liabilities, and the IDR975.0bn of related-party loans carried at face, are what make the equity worth more than the freight business alone. The discretionary IDR200.0bn buyback is disclosed but kept out of the bridge, because the engine divides by the pre-buyback share count.

The valuation arithmetic is the heart of the revision. The old EV/EBITDA leg applied the peer median to "LTM EBITDA" that was in fact FY2025A EBITDA of IDR269.4bn; the true trailing figure is the FY2025 number less the prior-year first half plus H1-2026, about three-fifths of it. The old P/B leg applied a fleet multiple to a book that is mostly cash and the related-party loan. Both legs are now zero-weighted: the DCF is the only reproducible value. The result is a base value of Rp1,947, rolled forward at the cost of equity to Rp2,198 and probability-weighted with the bear and bull to Rp2,613.

What moves the value is therefore specific. First, the pace and cost of the fleet build: FY2026E capex of IDR776.3bn and FY2027E capex of IDR804.4bn come before any contract revenue at scale, and every year of delay removes cash the market is already paying for. Second, the contract term: the agreement runs five years and no renewal is disclosed, so the base case re-contracts only half its volume after 2031; that is why four-fifths of the DCF enterprise value is terminal value and why the terminal assumption matters more than any single year. Third, the related-party receivable: it is performing and interest-bearing, but it is unsecured lending to the seller of the controlling stake, and its recovery is a governance question rather than a credit question [S6]. Bunker fuel is a fourth, smaller lever: at the deck's FY2026E Brent of US$96.0/bbl against FY2025A US$68.1/bbl, fuel is a direct margin hit because no contract carries a fuel clause [S6].

The rating boundary is explicit. A REDUCE needs a total return between a tenth and a quarter below the price; a SELL is anything worse than a quarter below. Our -36.7% return is well inside SELL, and it would take a bull case (full contract renewal and margin expansion) to reach today's price. The bull value of Rp4,789 is the upside case, not the base.

MBSS is an Indonesian sea-transport company for bulk mining cargo, principally thermal coal and, more recently, nickel. It moves coal from mine ports to discharge ports and to anchorage points for transhipment, operating a fleet of tugboats, barges and a mother vessel, with floating-crane transhipment offered as an integrated service [S2]. The fleet at 31 December 2025 was 33.0 barges, 18.0 tugboats and 1.0 vessel [S2, F1-F3], down from 44.0 barges and a larger tug fleet a year earlier after the 2025 disposal programme [S2, F4]. The longest barges in the fleet run to 365 ft and the most powerful tugs to 2,800 HP [S2, F55-F56].

The revenue model is a per-tonne sea-freight tariff. Voyage charters are priced per tonne for a specific voyage; time charters earn a hire rate over a period; both are recognised over the service period [S6]. That makes MBSS a volume times spread business, not a coal producer: it earns the freight margin on the tonne, bears the fuel, crew, docking, insurance and charter-in costs, and has no royalty or price exposure to the coal itself [S6]. Almost all revenue comes from the tugboat-and-barge segment, with a small floating-crane line and a single motor vessel [S2].

Indonesian coal moves from mine to power station or export vessel on a chain of trucks, barges and
transhipment cranes. The barging leg exists because river and coastal depths limit the size of vessel
that can load at the mine, so the operator with the right barge draft and the right transhipment
anchorage captures the freight. It is a capital-intensive service with few intellectual assets; the
durable advantages are fleet availability, safety records, customer relationships and the ability to
finance tonnage through a cycle.

The two disclosed customers above a tenth of revenue accounted for IDR169.7bn and IDR138.4bn of FY2025 revenue, from PT Sumber Daya Energi and PT Adaro Indonesia respectively [S6, F42-F43]. Customer concentration is therefore high in a book of IDR841.7bn, and the GEL contract is in part a diversification away from the two anchors. It is not a guarantee: GEL Group is a coal trader (jual beli batu bara, founded in 2013), not a producer, and no take-or-pay clause or disclosed cargo book sits behind the volume [S3]. If either anchor cuts volumes, or GEL's trading book is thinner than the contract, the revenue base funding the fleet build is smaller than the plan. Related-party revenue was 2.0% of the total in FY2025, down from the prior year [S6, F44], but related-party purchases were far larger.

The strategic reset is recent and explicit. The company describes the GEL contract as giving it a long-term volume base to move to the next stage of expansion [S3], and targets a significant fleet capacity increase in 2027, to be executed gradually and measured against utilisation [S3][S9]. The new controller, Wibowo Group Capital, has an investment in a company active in shipbuilding and ship maintenance [S8, F54], which is a natural source of expansion tonnage and also a related-party supply channel to watch. The board was replaced at an extraordinary general meeting on 17 September 2026, with Sugeng Pangraksa appointed president director [S11]. Management describes its priorities as customer continuity, safety and governance alongside growth [S11].

MBSS is a mid-sized operator in a fragmented field rather than the market leader. Its competitive position rests on three decades of coal-haulage experience since 1994 [S3], an integrated barge-plus- transhipment offer, and a customer base of large coal traders and producers [S6]. It does not own mines, terminals or dedicated port concessions, and it competes for tonnage with other Indonesian-flag barge owners, including the listed comparables we use in valuation [S0]. The group employed 183 people at the last count [S0] and is 90.1% owned by Wibowo Group Capital after the tender offer [S8, F40], with the public holding the remainder.

Indonesian coal supply is set by the government's annual work plan and budget quota. The 2026 coal RKAB was set at 600 Mt and was then relaxed toward 700 Mt to capture higher prices [S12, S13, F34-F35]. The energy minister cited a price of US$154.0/t for 6,330 kcal/kg GAR coal in October 2026, with thermal coal at a multi-year high [S13, F36]. Our coal deck holds Newcastle 6,000 kcal/kg NAR at US$118/t for FY2027E against a spot print of US$150/t and an FY2025A average of US$108/t, and the Indonesian HBA reference at US$112/t [coal deck].

The link from the coal deck to this company is demand, not price. MBSS buys no coal and sells no coal: its tariff is a per-tonne freight rate agreed per voyage or per charter [S6], so the model's coal-cost share is zero and no coal driver reaches revenue or costs. That is a deliberate choice, not an omission: a higher coal price lifts miners' willingness to move tonnes, which we capture in the volume path, but it does not change the freight rate on a signed contract. The desk's view that the war-premium carry in spot is not a level to extrapolate therefore enters through the demand-side volume risk in the bear case, not through a price-linked revenue line. The base value is unchanged at the deck's US$118/t and at the spot print of US$150/t because neither is an input to the P&L [S6, coal deck].

The demand side has two legs. Domestic coal demand for power stations is stabilised by the Domestic Market Obligation policy, which the company describes as a mechanism that keeps distribution continuity and gives barge operators a steadier volume base [S2]. The export leg depends on Chinese and Indian thermal-coal demand and on Indonesian miners' ability to move tonnes to anchorage. The company also reports a growing nickel logistics book as smelters, including HPAL and RKEF plants, expand in Sulawesi [S2]. That nickel diversification is the same trend the desk favours in nickel supply-discipline names, and it gives MBSS a second cargo stream when coal volumes are flat.

The 2027 contract sits exactly on this policy axis. At 6.0 Mt a year it is equivalent to about four per cent of the coal allocated to the national power utility's 2026 requirement, by the company's own framing, and it serves both domestic and export buyers with loading in Riau, Jambi and South Sumatra [S3, S10]. The contract is for five years with no disclosed take-or-pay mechanism; the company says realisation depends on service execution and transported volume [S3][S10]. That is the central industry fact for this name: a long-term volume agreement improves planning and financing, but it is not a guaranteed revenue line.

Competition is fragmented and largely price-based. The listed barge and coal-logistics names - Trans Power Marine, Dana Brata Luhur, Dwi Guna Laksana, Pelita Samudera Shipping and BBRM - compete for the same coal and nickel cargo, and the peer set in valuation is drawn from their market pricing [S0]. Barriers to entry are capital and relationships rather than technology; a well-financed entrant can buy or build barges, and the new controller's shipbuilding interest lowers that barrier for MBSS specifically. Supplier power sits with shipyards, fuel suppliers and the owners of chartered-in tonnage; MBSS chartered in IDR152.3bn of vessel capacity in FY2025, about a quarter of direct costs [S6, F12], so it is both a customer of and a competitor to the same fleet owners. Buyer power is high because a handful of coal traders and miners control the cargo, and the two largest customers are disclosed above [S6].

The moat is therefore modest. MBSS has scale in a niche, an integrated transhipment capability and long customer tenure, but no resource, port or technology exclusivity, and its margins are exposed to fuel and to the charter-in market. In a five-forces frame, rivalry and buyer power are high, supplier power is medium-high on fuel and tonnage, new-entry is medium, and substitution is low in the near term because no alternative moves bulk coal at barge economics for these routes. The market position supports a going concern, not pricing power [S2, S6].

External influences are threefold. Coal policy - RKAB quotas, DMO and export rules - sets the volume through the system [S12, S13]. Oil sets the largest controllable cost through bunker fuel, with Brent at US$84.0/bbl in our deck against US$118/bbl spot [oil deck]. And the rupiah sets the cost base: with the rupiah at Rp18,350/USD in the macro deck, dollar-linked vessel, fuel and docking costs translate into a higher rupiah cost base even when tariffs are slow to follow [macro deck]. The coal deck has Newcastle flat-to-down from FY2026E and the macro deck has a weakening rupiah, a combination that is a headwind for a rupiah-cost, dollar-revenue-adjacent business.

The five-year record is one of a shrinking, then stabilising, operating business underneath a growing balance sheet. Revenue fell from IDR1,374.9bn in FY2022 to IDR964.0bn in FY2023 and IDR830.5bn in FY2024 before edging up to IDR841.7bn in FY2025 [S0, S6, F16]. The FY2022-FY2023 profit line is not comparable with later years because the direct-cost method hides depreciation inside cost of revenue; we restated D&A from the audited financial statements to IDR20.5bn and IDR12.7bn for those years and IDR149.5bn and IDR81.2bn for the last two [S6, F9-F10][S14, F51-F52]. On that basis FY2025 EBITDA was IDR269.4bn, a 32.0% margin, against IDR350.5bn in FY2024 [S6]. The headline net profit of IDR370.2bn is not the operating result: it includes IDR129.8bn of interest income, an IDR95.7bn gain on vessel disposals and a foreign-exchange gain, against IDR188.1bn of EBIT [S6, F19, F25].

H1-2026 is the important recent read, and it is why the trailing figure is far below FY2025. Revenue fell to IDR406.9bn from the prior-year first half, gross profit fell to IDR91.4bn and G&A rose to IDR48.2bn [S5, F27, F46, F47]. With depreciation of IDR37.8bn inside direct costs, the first half earned an EBITDA margin near a fifth of revenue [S5, F30]. Two costs explain the squeeze. Fuel was IDR75.3bn in the half [S5, F29], and vessel charter-in rose to IDR102.4bn from the prior-year period as the company rented capacity to cover work while its owned fleet was smaller [S5, F28]. The revenue fall is volume and mix; the cost rise is fuel at a higher Brent and charter-in that is structural until the owned fleet is delivered.

The trailing twelve-month figure the old valuation should have used is therefore not FY2025A. FY2025A EBITDA of IDR269.4bn less the prior-year first half (gross profit IDR184.4bn less G&A IDR40.2bn plus depreciation IDR43.0bn) plus the current first half (gross profit IDR91.4bn less G&A IDR48.2bn plus depreciation IDR37.8bn) is materially lower than the last actual year, at about three-fifths of it. That is the denominator the sector card requires for a cyclical: a trailing, not a peak-year, number. It is also why we do not use an EV/EBITDA cross-check at all: applying a current-year multiple to FY2025A EBITDA would repeat the procyclical error the card forbids [S5, S6, F27-F30, F46-F47, F58-F60].

The cost base is dominated by four lines in FY2025: vessel charter at IDR152.3bn (a related-party line), fuel at IDR149.6bn, vessel operations, and D&A. Fuel is the only material oil-linked input, and it was 25.0% of cost of revenue - the parameter we drive off the Brent deck [S6, F11]. There is no fuel surcharge or indexation disclosed in the charter contracts [S6], so a rise in Brent flows straight to the margin. That is the mechanism by which our FY2026E gross margin falls from the FY2025 base: the FY2026E input margin of 29.0% is the H1-2026 actual cost base, and the deck's Brent at US$96.0/bbl against US$68.1/bbl in FY2025A takes the reported margin down again [oil deck]. From FY2027E the deck's Brent falls and the owned fleet replaces charter-in, so the input margin returns to the FY2025 actual of about a third; we assume no margin expansion above it.

The balance sheet is the strongest part of the story and the hardest to value cleanly. At 30 June 2026 the company held IDR2,143.7bn of cash against IDR530.6bn of BCA bank loans, all rupiah investment credit secured on 29.0 vessels vessels, and IDR4.0bn of current plus IDR2.1bn of non-current lease liabilities, giving net cash and a comfortable debt-service position [S5, F32, F48, F50, F61, F62]. It also carries IDR975.0bn of long-term loans to related parties: IDR635.0bn to PT Galley Adhika Arnawama, the seller of the controlling stake, and IDR340.0bn to PT Anaga Group Indonesia, both at 8.5%, with the Anaga loan due on 22 December 2030 [S6, F13-F15, F57]. That receivable is about a fifth of total assets, is unsecured on the disclosed terms, and generated a large part of the interest income that makes the profit line look better than the operating business [S6, F19, F45]. We carry it at face in the bridge and forecast its 8.5% coupon in the non-operating line: the loan note [S6] discloses the principal, rate and maturities but no security, arrears, impairment allowance or expected credit loss, so there is no sourced loss given default, and the full coupon is the consistent treatment. Non-recovery is a bear-case overlay, sized in the scenario section, not a base-case deduction [S6, F13-F15, F57]. H1-2026 interest income already includes the coupon, and a deposit-only yield would understate earnings by roughly that amount [S5, S6].

Cash conversion is weak against reported profit. FY2025 free cash flow to the firm was IDR-100.8bn on IDR269.4bn of EBITDA, after IDR370.2bn of vessel purchases [S0, S6, F22]; the net profit of IDR370.2bn was supported by interest income and the disposal gain, not by freight cash. In H1-2026 the company spent IDR372.8bn acquiring vessels [S5, F31], more than the whole of FY2025, and funded it from cash and new bank drawings [S5, F32]. This is the definition of a growth-capex year: the fleet build is real, and it is why our forecast free cash flow to the firm is negative through FY2028E and turns positive at IDR309.9bn in FY2029E.

Our forecast reflects the contract. We model revenue at IDR862.5bn in FY2026E, up 2.5% on FY2025, then IDR1,462.6bn in FY2027E as half the contract is served and IDR2,062.5bn in FY2028E as the full 6.0 Mt is added to the existing book, reaching IDR2,062.5bn by FY2030E [S3, S5]. After the five-year term we re-contract only half the contract volume, so FY2032E revenue falls to IDR1,462.5bn; that renewal haircut is the single largest assumption in the valuation. EBITDA is IDR176.2bn in FY2026E and IDR619.4bn in FY2028E; EPS is Rp118 and Rp255 respectively. Capex is IDR776.3bn in FY2026E and IDR804.4bn in FY2027E before falling to replacement level (12.0% of revenue) from FY2030E. Net borrowing is zero in the base: the company has the cash and IDR500.0bn and IDR360.0bn BCA facilities to fund the build without an equity issue [S5, F33, F49]. We pay no dividend, matching the FY2024 resolution to retain all profit [S2], and equity compounds to IDR5,786.2bn by FY2030E.

Earnings quality is mixed and needs stating plainly. The 2025 extension of barge and tug useful lives to 20.0 years years cut the depreciation charge [S6, F26], which flatters EBITDA versus FY2024 without changing cash. Vessel disposals generated gains of IDR95.7bn in FY2025 [S6, F25], and the company has been both a seller and a buyer of tonnage within two years, so the other line is an operating-financing hybrid that we exclude from forecasts. Interest income on related-party loans supports net profit but not the freight business [S6, F45]; we now include the 8.5% coupon in the non-operating line but keep it out of FCFF, because the loan principal is carried separately in the bridge. Return on equity falls to 5.1% in FY2026E from 10.0% in FY2025 because the forecast carries no vessel-disposal gains, the equity base includes the cash and the loan, and the new fleet depreciates before it earns. The freight business earns a freight return, not a deposit return, and the reported FY2025 ROE is the wrong benchmark for the forecast. The accruals position is not alarming - net profit is close to operating cash flow once the disposal gain is removed - but the quality of the reported profit is lower than the headline margin suggests, and the net profit line should be read as a financing result as much as a freight result.

The buyback is disclosed but not assumed in the valuation. The company announced up to IDR200.0bn of buybacks, equivalent to 42.2 m shares outstanding shares, running from 22 October to 31 December 2026 [S4, F37, F38]. The programme is discretionary and was not executed at the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date, and the engine's per-share divisor is the pre-buyback balance-sheet count, so we keep the pre-buyback cash and the pre-buyback count together rather than deduct the cash against the wrong divisor. At our intrinsic value the repurchase would destroy value - it buys shares at Rp4,130 that we think are worth Rp1,947 - so full execution at the market price would take a few per cent off the per-share value, not add to it; that is the disclosed cost of leaving the discretionary programme outside the bridge. Dividend capacity exists: FY2029E free cash flow of IDR309.9bn covers about two-thirds of the IDR464.5bn of net profit, and a one-third payout would be a low-single-digit yield on today's price, but the company pays none and the new controller's priority is fleet capacity [S3, S9].

We use a free-cash-flow-to-firm DCF as the only valuation method, weighted 100.0%. That is a deliberate narrowing. A capital-intensive, asset-backed service business with a finite contract book and a large financial-asset balance is exactly the case for a DCF: the value is the cash the fleet and the contract produce, plus the financial assets the company owns. The two multiple cross-checks the house normally uses do not survive contact with the facts. EV/EBITDA would apply a current-year multiple to FY2025A EBITDA, which the commodity-cyclical card forbids and which the trailing figure shows is too high; P/B would apply a fleet-peer book multiple to total equity that is mostly cash and the related-party loan, double-counting assets the bridge already carries at face. We therefore zero-weight both and disclose the arithmetic rather than publish a blend that cannot be reproduced. A NAV or reserve-based method does not apply because MBSS owns no resource; a P/E anchor does not apply because earnings are dominated by interest income, disposal gains and FX, none of which is the freight business.

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck. The risk-free rate is the IDR government bond yield of 7.4% less the sovereign default spread of 1.6%, an equity risk premium of 4.2% plus an Indonesia country premium of 2.5%, and an unlevered beta of 1.00 (the industry default; no COAL_LOGISTICS regression exists) levered to 1.06 at the market debt-to-equity ratio of 7.4%. That gives a cost of equity of 12.9%; with pre-tax debt at 9.4%, the WACC is 12.5%. The rupiah weakness in the macro deck raises the nominal rate but also raises nominal tariffs and costs; we keep the real framework consistent through the deck.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR843.7bn; adding net cash (the IDR2,143.7bn cash balance less IDR530.6bn of bank loans and IDR4.0bn plus IDR2.1bn of lease liabilities), the IDR975.0bn related-party loan at face, and deducting minorities gives Rp1,947 per share on the pre-buyback 1,750 m shares. No credit allowance and no buyback deduction are applied, for the sourcing and divisor reasons set out above. Three features drive the result. First, free cash flow is negative in FY2026E-FY2028E while the fleet is built, so the explicit-period present value is small. Second, 80.1% of the enterprise value sits in the terminal value, which capitalises the post-2031 business at a 12.5% discount rate and 2.5% long-run growth; we assume only half the GEL contract is re-contracted after its fixed term because no renewal is disclosed, which is the re-contracting haircut a finite contract requires. Third, the bridge adds the IDR975.0bn related-party loan at face, the largest single non-operating item after cash; the bear case sizes the non-recovery risk outside the model because the engine cannot vary the bridge by scenario.

The cross-checks are explained rather than weighted, and excluded from value. On EV/EBITDA, the peer set is Trans Power Marine, Dana Brata Luhur, Dwi Guna Laksana, Pelita Samudera Shipping and BBRM [S0]. The engine's three-name median was a median of three observations, and PSSI carries no EV/EBITDA in the pack, so it was effectively Trans Power Marine alone. Adding house-covered BBRM - which the original set omitted without a stated reason - gives a four-name median of about seven times and a range from about three to about thirteen times; PSSI carries no EV/EBITDA in the pack. The earlier exclusion rationale was also wrong: BESS trades far above the range, not at the mid-thirties multiple quoted, and ALII's multiple is positive, not absent. Even at the low end of the range, applying a multiple to FY2025A EBITDA would value the peak year, so the right answer is not a better peer median but no multiple leg. Shown as unweighted references, the median applied to the trailing EBITDA of IDR269.4bn less the half-year swing values the shares roughly a tenth above our DCF of Rp1,947, and the same multiple on last-actual EBITDA values them about a third above it; both remain below the market price, and the operating-book P/B reference sits between the two. None is an input to the target. The P/B cross-check has the same problem in a different place: at the peer multiple it values the cash and the related-party loan at more than face, on top of the bridge that already counts them.

The sensitivity grid shows the DCF per share is more sensitive to WACC and terminal growth than to any single operating input over the plausible range, which is typical of a long-duration, asset-heavy business with a terminal-heavy value. The twelve-month value grid shows that even a four-point addition to revenue growth every year and a two-point margin improvement leaves the value below the current price, which tells us the market is pricing more than our central case can support.

The reverse DCF makes the gap explicit. Holding our WACC, terminal growth, capex and payout, the current price implies FY2027E revenue growth of 89.4% against our 69.6%: the market needs the contract to ramp materially faster than the fleet build allows, with no capex overrun and no fuel squeeze. Today's price is 35.1x FY2026E EV/EBITDA, 10.6x FY2028E EV/EBITDA and 1.8x P/B, with a dividend yield of 0.0% [S0].

Our target is built bottom-up. The DCF value is Rp1,947; rolling it forward one year at the cost of equity gives Rp2,198 for the base case; weighting bear, base and bull at the scenario probabilities gives Rp2,613, which we publish as Rp2,613. No liquidity discount is applied because the three-month traded value is above the house floor, but the free float has fallen to about a tenth of the shares after the tender offer [S8, F40] and the buyback can take it close to the exchange minimum [S4, F38]; a liquidity premium could re-emerge if the block overhang clears and volumes fall.

The largest downside risk is contract execution: the GEL agreement is a five-year volume plan, not a take-or-pay revenue guarantee, and the company itself says realisation depends on service and volume [S3, S10]. Likelihood high, impact high. Second is the fleet build: to serve the contract the company must add tonnage, and its own H1-2026 capex of IDR372.8bn [S5] shows how much cash that can absorb; a delay or cost overrun pushes free cash flow out and may require debt beyond the BCA headroom [S5, F33, F49]. Likelihood medium, impact high. Third is fuel: with no pass-through clause and 25.0% of cost of revenue oil-linked [S6, F11], a renewed Brent spike of the kind the deck already carries for FY2026E is a direct margin hit. Likelihood medium, impact medium.

The governance risks are specific and could be more damaging than the operating ones. The IDR975.0bn of related-party loans [S6, F13] sit with the seller of the control block and its affiliates; if they are not repaid on schedule, the market will re-price the receivable and the cash quality together. Likelihood medium, impact high. The new controller holds 90.1% [S8], the public float is near the minimum, and the company is buying back stock [S4]; the combination raises the prospect of low free float, index exclusion and a change in the board's accountability to minority holders [S11]. Likelihood medium, impact medium. Customer concentration is the third governance-adjacent risk: Sumber Daya Energi and Adaro are IDR169.7bn and IDR138.4bn of revenue [S6, F42-F43], and GEL is a trader with no disclosed cargo book [S3]; the loss of either anchor or a GEL shortfall is a direct hit to the revenue base funding the fleet. We carry that in the bear. Coal demand and Chinese policy are the sector's standard cycle risks: the RKAB relaxation to 700 Mt [S12] supports volume now but a coal-price slide would compress miners' margins and could reduce the tonnage offered to barge operators. Likelihood medium, impact medium. Rupiah depreciation at the deck's Rp18,350/USD helps dollar-indexed tariffs but raises the rupiah cost of imported vessel and fuel inputs; on balance a modest negative. Regulatory changes to RKAB, DMO or export proceeds retention are low-likelihood, medium-impact events for a transporter that is not a royalty payer.

Our bear case assumes the contract is a volume aspiration rather than contracted revenue, the fleet build slips, the anchors cut volumes, charter-in costs stay at the H1-2026 level and the related-party receivable is questioned; it values the shares at Rp1,267. The base case assumes half the contract is served in FY2027, the full 6.0 Mt from FY2028, no margin expansion above the FY2025 actual, half the contract re-contracted after 2031, and values the shares at Rp2,198. The bull case assumes the full contract is served from the owned fleet, renewed in full at expiry, with the related-party loans repaid in full and a dividend after the build; it values the shares at Rp4,789, the only scenario above today's price. The operating shocks are mirrored - ten points of revenue growth and ten points of gross margin either way - and the probabilities are 25.0% bear, 50.0% base and 25.0% bull.

The bear is a trough-margin bear, not a mild haircut: the gross-margin shock takes EBITDA back to the H1-2026 trough and the revenue shock removes the contract ramp and part of the existing book. The IDR975.0bn related-party loan is carried at face in the bridge in every scenario because the engine's scenario framework cannot vary the bridge, so the bear's non-recovery is sized here as an overlay rather than inside the scenario value: a quarter write-down would remove about an eighth of the bear equity value and a full write-off about half, equivalent to a quarter of the IDR975.0bn balance across 1,750 m shares. Both are disclosed, not modelled. There is no share-count shock: the engine holds the pre-buyback share count and the discretionary buyback is outside the bridge, so an unfunded rights issue or further repurchase is not claimed as a value driver. The mirror is honest on the operating drivers; the asymmetry between the bull and the bear comes from the terminal renewal and the capex, both of which are sourced to the contract term rather than chosen.

Signposts that would change the view: a take-or-pay or minimum-volume clause added to the GEL contract would move the bear case toward the base; evidence that the new build is delivered at the controller's shipyard at cost and on schedule would improve capex and margin; repayment of the related-party loans would remove the largest governance discount; a decision to pay out the excess cash would change the dividend-capacity anchor. Conversely, a first full-year report with negative operating cash flow and rising charter-in costs would confirm the bear.

Ownership has just changed. PT Wibowo Group Capital acquired 82.5% from PT Galley Adhika Arnawama in July 2026 for IDR4,200.0bn, equal to Rp2,915/share, and its mandatory tender offer completed on 15 October 2026 at the same price, lifting it to 90.1% [S7, S8, F39-F41]. The remaining shares are held by the public, a float of roughly a tenth before the buyback. The company's buyback runs from 22 October to 31 December 2026 for up to IDR200.0bn, equivalent to 42.2 m shares [S4, F37-F38], and management states it will keep the free float within the rules [S4]. The exchange's minimum free float is a live constraint for a name at this ownership level, not background noise.

The board was replaced at the extraordinary general meeting on 17 September 2026, with Sugeng Pangraksa as president director and a new board of commissioners; the company thanked the outgoing board for its service [S11]. A full board change at the same time as a change of control is normal after an acquisition, but it removes institutional memory at the moment the company is committing to a large fleet build, and it concentrates decision-making in the controller.

Related-party dealings are the main governance exposure. At 31 December 2025 the company had IDR975.0bn of long-term loans to related parties: IDR635.0bn to the former controller and IDR340.0bn to an affiliate, both at 8.5%, with the affiliate loan due on 22 December 2030 [S6, F13-F15, F57]. It also had related-party other receivables, related-party trade payables and an IDR152.3bn related-party vessel charter cost in FY2025 [S6, F12]. Related-party sales were 2.0% of revenue [S6, F44]. The new controller's shipbuilding and ship-maintenance investment [S8, F54] creates a further related-party channel for the 2027 fleet expansion. None of this is a finding of wrongdoing; it is a structure in which the controller is both the lender's counterparty, the charter counterparty and potentially the supplier of the new fleet, and minority holders have limited ability to price those flows.

The buyback deserves its own line because it is sometimes called value-neutral. It is not: at Rp4,130 the company is repurchasing shares the DCF values at Rp1,947, so full execution would transfer value from continuing holders to sellers. We disclose it but do not put it in the bridge, because the programme is discretionary and the engine divides by the pre-buyback share count; full execution at the market price would take a few per cent off the per-share value, and that cost is disclosed rather than silently assumed away [S4, F37, F38].

On the formal checks: the auditor for FY2025 was Tanubrata Sutanto Fahmi Bambang & Rekan [S2], and the audited financial statements carry an independent auditor's report [S6]. We found no disclosure of pledged controlling shares in the 2025 annual report or the interim accounts - none found, checked. The dividend record is nil: the FY2024 AGM resolved not to distribute a dividend and to retain the profit [S2], and no FY2025 dividend has been declared [S0]. Earnings quality is optics-class rather than manipulation-class: the useful-life extension [S6, F26], the disposal gains [S6, F25] and the interest income from related-party loans [S6, F45] are all disclosed and all flatter the headline; we restate and exclude them from the freight operating view. There is no evidence of fabricated revenue or fictitious cash.

ESG exposures are those of a coal-logistics operator. The company's revenue is tied to thermal coal, which carries transition risk as power markets decarbonise, mitigated only partly by the nickel cargo diversification [S2]. Operational risks are vessel safety, spills and crew welfare, managed under ISM and ISPS standards with a board-level safety and compliance oversight described in the annual report [S2]. We do not apply a separate ESG valuation penalty; the risk is carried in the bear case through volume and contract-renewal assumptions.

The dated catalysts are the buyback completing at the end of 2026 [S4], the FY2026 audited results by the end of the first quarter of 2027 [S2], the first fleet deliveries and the GEL ramp through 2027 [S3, S9], and the floating-stock constraint that comes with a controlling owner above 90.1% [S8]. The related-party loan maturities fall in 2029 and 2030 [S6, F14-F15], which sets the long stop for the receivable question.

The KPIs we will monitor between updates are the contracted and realised tonnage, the average tariff per tonne, fleet utilisation and the number of barges in service, the charter-in cost line as a share of revenue, fuel cost per tonne, capex per delivered vessel, operating cash flow against reported profit, net cash, the related-party loan balance and interest received, and the free float. Any one of these can move the thesis; the one that matters most is whether the GEL volume shows up in revenue at a margin that covers the cost of the new fleet [S3, S5].

bear.narrative: The GEL contract is a volume aspiration rather than take-or-pay: realisations track service and cargo availability [S3], the 2027 fleet build slips, and only about half the contracted 6 Mt/yr is ever moved; the two anchors, Sumber Daya Energi (20.2% of FY2025 revenue) and Adaro (16.4%), cut volumes as coal prices fall [S6, F42, F43]. Charter-in costs stay high while the owned fleet is delivered late, so the gross margin stays at the H1-2026 trough and EBITDA is near a fifth of revenue [S5, F27-F30, F46, F47]. The IDR975bn related-party loans are questioned and part of the principal is not recovered [S6, F13]; the engine's bridge cannot vary by scenario, so the base carries the loans at face and the report sizes the non-recovery overlay here rather than in the scenario value. The free float is near the exchange minimum after the tender offer [S8], and the discretionary buyback is not assumed to complete.

bull.narrative: The GEL contract ramps faster than modelled and is renewed at expiry: the new controller's shipbuilding interests deliver barges on schedule and at cost, so the full 6 Mt/yr is served from the owned fleet with high utilisation, and the 2% related-party revenue base plus new coal traders diversify the book. The 8.50% related-party loans are repaid into the company and fund the build without debt, full recovery confirms the face value the base already carries, and the announced buyback plus a post-2031 dividend return capital; the contract's volume gives pricing power on the next round of long-term charters. The share count is held at the pre-buyback 1,750.0m because the engine cannot fund a further repurchase.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +2.5%: H1-2026 revenue was IDR 406.9bn [S5, F27] and Q2-2026 alone was IDR 227.8bn, so a second half at the Q2 run-rate gives IDR 862.5bn (406.9 + 2 x 227.8) against FY2025's IDR 841.7bn [S6, F16]; the H1 average would give only 813.8bn, and we take the latest quarter rather than the half because Q2 is the post-reorganisation run-rate. FY2027E +69.6%: the five-year GEL Group contract signed on 26 October 2026 covers 500,000 t/month (6 Mt/yr, 30 Mt in total) with potential average revenue of Rp1.2trn/yr, i.e. about Rp200k/t [S3, F5-F8]; the company states the 2027 capacity expansion is gradual and measured [S3, S9], so we serve half the contract (3 Mt, IDR600bn) in FY2027 as the first barges are delivered, with the rest chartered in. FY2028E +41.0%: the full 6 Mt (IDR1,200bn) is served on top of the existing IDR862.5bn business, the level the red team derived and the contract states [S3, F6, F8]. FY2029E-FY2031E 0%: the contract is a fixed 6 Mt/yr with no escalation and the existing book is held flat, because no volume growth is disclosed for either. FY2032E -29.1%: the GEL contract has a fixed five-year term and no renewal or extension is disclosed [S3], so we re-contract only half its volume (3 Mt, IDR600bn) after 2031 and retain the existing IDR862.5bn business; this is the renewal haircut the red team required, with full renewal in the bull case and no renewal in the bear. FY2033E-FY2035E 0%: the retained business is held flat; 2.5% long-run growth applies only after the explicit period.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 29.0% reflects the H1-2026 run-rate, not a haircut: H1-2026 gross profit was IDR 91.4bn on revenue IDR 406.9bn, a 22.5% reported margin with vessel charter-in up to IDR 102.4bn from IDR 75.9bn and fuel at IDR 75.3bn [S5, F27, F28, F29, F46]. At the FY2026E Brent deck of USD96 against FY2025A USD68.1, the 25%-of-COGS fuel link takes 29.0% down to about 22%, reproducing the H1 actual. From FY2027E we restore the FY2025 base margin of 30.0-32.0% as the deck's Brent falls to USD84 and the owned fleet replaces charter-in capacity; no margin expansion above the FY2025 actual (32.0% on IDR 269.1bn gross profit, [S6, F16-F17]) is assumed for the GEL volume, which also requires the new fleet. Scale economies and higher utilisation stay in the bull case.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Zero: MBSS buys no coal. Its direct costs are vessel charter, bunker fuel, vessel operations, depreciation, crew, spares and insurance [S6 p.56]. The Newcastle price affects barging demand and tariffs, carried in the revenue path, not a cost line.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Zero because link1_share is zero: there is no coal-linked cost to pass through. Tariff linkage to the coal cycle is captured in revenue growth [S6 p.56].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Bunker fuel was IDR 149.6bn of FY2025 direct costs of IDR 572.7bn, 26.1% [S6, F11]; in H1-2026 fuel was IDR 75.3bn of IDR 315.5bn, 23.8% [S5, F29]. We use 25%, the midpoint, as the share of cost of revenue exposed to Brent. Fuel is the only material oil-linked line.

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Zero: the annual report and LK disclose no fuel-surcharge or index-linked bunker clause in the voyage and time-charter contracts; tariffs are per tonne agreed per voyage or per charter [S6 p.218-219]. Fuel therefore hits the margin, which is why the FY2026E margin falls.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 11.8% holds the H1-2026 actual (IDR 48.2bn on revenue IDR 406.9bn), which already includes the change-of-control process costs [S5, F47, F27]; we do not assume they reverse inside the year. FY2027E 10.5% and FY2028E 10.0% reflect the same rupiah cost base spread over the GEL contract volume (a fixed-cost dilution, not a cut); from FY2029E 9.5% returns to the FY2025 actual of 9.6% (IDR 80.9bn) [S6, F18] as the contract reaches full run-rate.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: FY2025 D&A was IDR 81.2bn, 9.6% of revenue [S6, F9], not the IDR 5.6bn in the Yahoo pack, and FY2024 was IDR 149.5bn before the barge and tug useful lives were extended from 16 to 20 years [S6, F10, F26]. FY2026E 10.5% keeps the charge and adds the vessels bought in H1-2026 (IDR 372.8bn [S5, F31]); FY2027E 12.0% adds a full year of the expansion fleet; the ratio settles at 11.0% from FY2028E as the asset base and revenue grow together.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 90%: MBSS spent IDR 372.8bn acquiring vessels in H1-2026 [S5, F31] against IDR 370.2bn for the whole of FY2025 [S6, F22], and the company states a significant fleet expansion in 2027 to serve the GEL contract [S3, S9]. FY2027E 55% and FY2028E 30% carry the build; FY2029E-FY2030E fall to 14%/12%, replacement level just above the 11% D&A ratio. From FY2031E we set 14.25% of revenue, not 12%: terminal capex must fund replacement (11% of revenue, the D&A ratio) plus growth times asset intensity, and with PP&E at about 1.3x revenue [S0, S6] the 2.5% terminal growth needs a further 3.25% of revenue, so 14.25% keeps the terminal cash flow internally consistent instead of under-funding growth. The barges date from the 2010s (44 in 2024, 33 after the 2025 sale [S2, F4]).

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital was IDR 110.1bn on revenue of IDR 841.7bn, 13.1% [S0]; H1-2026 receivables include a related-party balance that does not scale with revenue, so we use the FY2025 ratio and do not extrapolate the Q2-2026 jump.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Total FY2025 tax was final tax of IDR 10.1bn plus income tax of IDR 31.8bn on pre-tax profit of IDR 402.7bn, 10.4% [S6 p.6]; H1-2026 final tax was IDR 4.9bn on revenue of IDR 406.9bn [S5 p.7]. Set 10% on pre-tax profit.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The BCA investment-credit facilities carry 7.75-8.00% per annum and are secured on 29 vessels [S5, F50; S5 p.56]. FY2025 finance costs of IDR 24.7bn on opening debt of IDR 352.5bn imply 7.0% [S6, F20]. Set 8.0% on opening debt.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 blended interest income of IDR 129.8bn is the income on bank deposits and the IDR 975bn of long-term loans to related parties at 8.50% [S6, F19, F13, F45], so dividing it by cash alone would overstate the deposit rate. The LK's time deposits carried rates up to 6.0% [S6 p.45]; set 4.5% on the cash balance, in line with IDR deposit rates.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero net new borrowing in the base case: the company held IDR 2.14trn of cash at 30 June 2026 [S5, F48] and had drawn IDR 530.6bn of the BCA investment facilities [S5, F32], leaving headroom under the Rp500bn and Rp360bn facilities [S5, F33, F49]. We assume the build is funded from cash and the existing facilities rather than a new equity raise; a rights issue is left to the bear case.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: The 8.50% coupon on the IDR975bn long-term loans to related parties is real, contracted and interest-bearing cash [S6, F13, F14, F15, F57], so it is forecast: IDR82.9bn a year on the full balance to FY2029E, then IDR28.9bn in FY2030E on the IDR340bn Anaga loan that matures on 22 December 2030 [S6, F15, F57]. H1-2026 interest income of IDR70.1bn already includes the coupon [S5], and the engine's cash_yield line applies a deposit rate to cash only, so this is the one non-operating line through which the receivable's return can reach the P&L. Disposal gains (IDR49.1bn and IDR95.7bn in FY2024-FY2025, F25) are lumpy and are not forecast; the company is adding vessels, not selling them.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took 0.19% of FY2025 net profit (IDR 0.7bn of IDR 370.9bn) [S6 p.6]; the group's two subsidiaries are 99%-owned after the MASS and MGSS buy-ins [S6 p.11]. Set 0.2%.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Nil in the base case and in every explicit forecast year: the FY2024 AGM resolved not to distribute a dividend and retained the full IDR295bn [S2 p.119], no FY2025 dividend has been declared, and the new controller's stated priority is fleet capacity for the GEL contract [S3, S9]. The report shows dividend capacity at through-cycle free cash flow and the yield a one-third payout would support; a dividend initiation is a post-2031 event in the bull case, outside the explicit window, because the fleet build and the IDR975bn receivable maturities absorb the cash until then.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero in every year. The buyback of up to 42.17m shares (2.41% of the 1,750.0m outstanding at 31 December 2025) announced on 21 October 2026 runs only to 31 December 2026 and is discretionary [S4, F21, F37, F38]; it was not executed at the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date and the engine's per-share divisor is the pre-buyback balance-sheet count. We therefore keep the pre-buyback cash and the pre-buyback count together rather than pair a cash deduction with the wrong divisor; the report shows the pro-forma per-share effect of full execution as a disclosed sensitivity. No rights issue or further buyback is announced or assumed in the base [S4].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5%: Bank Indonesia's long-run inflation target midpoint for rupiah cash flows [macro deck inflation_idr_lt], a mature maritime-logistics business growing with Indonesian coal volume after the explicit years. Below the 3% explicit long-run revenue growth and well below the contract-ramp years.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check applies the 7.44x peer median to 'LTM EBITDA of IDR269.4bn', but 269.4 is FY2025A. True LTM = FY2025A 269.4 - H1-2025 186.8 (GP 184.44 - G&A 40.17 + D&A 42.54) + H1-2026 80.97 (91.40 - 48.20 + 37.77) = IDR163.5bn [S5, S6, F27-F30, F46-F47]. At 7.44x that is IDR1,216bn EV, IDR3,779bn equity, Rp2,159/share, not Rp2,609; the 30% method weight loses ~Rp450/share and the target falls to ~Rp2,950 (TR -28.6%, SELL). The industry card also forbids current-year multiples for a cyclical.
challenges.answer: The 269.4 figure was FY2025A, not LTM. The trailing figure is FY2025A EBITDA less the prior-year first half plus H1-2026, i.e. 269.4 - (184.44 - 40.17 + 42.98) + (91.40 - 48.20 + 37.77) = 163.1, about three-fifths of the last actual year [S5, S6, F27-F30, F46-F47, F58-F60]. The engine's EV/EBITDA leg applies last-actual EBITDA and has no LTM metric input, so rather than leave a 65%-too-high denominator in the blend we zero-weight both multiple legs and value on the DCF alone; the report discloses the LTM arithmetic and no longer labels FY2025A as LTM. The rating is re-tested at the corrected value: target Rp2,327, TR -43.7%, SELL.

challenges.challenge: The 7.44x 'peer median' is the median of n=3: TPMA 7.44x, TEBE 12.91x, DWGL 3.04x; PSSI has no EV/EBITDA in the peer block, so the median is TPMA alone. BBRM (house coverage, COAL_LOGISTICS, 4.59x in `cov_publish comps`) is omitted from the peer set without explanation, and PSSI's 4.42x is not the input. The assumptions' exclusion rationale is also wrong: BESS is 84.6x not 35x, and ALII is 28.6x positive, not 'no positive EV/EBITDA'.
challenges.answer: The peer set is now TPMA, TEBE, DWGL, PSSI and BBRM; the current data pack has TPMA 7.44x, TEBE 12.91x, DWGL 3.04x and BBRM 6.68x, a four-name median of 7.06x and a range of 3.04-12.91x (PSSI carries no EV/EBITDA; the published BBRM snapshot's 4.59x is a price-date difference from the 6.68x pack value). This is disclosed in valuation.peers_note. BBRM is house-covered COAL_LOGISTICS and its omission was unsupported; it is now included. The exclusion rationale is corrected: BESS is 84.6x, not 35x, and ALII is 28.6x positive, not "no positive EV/EBITDA". Because the EV leg is zero-weighted after C1, we do not publish a method value at each multiple: applying any multiple to FY2025A EBITDA would repeat the peak-year error, so the values would not be used in the target and would only mislead.

challenges.challenge: P/B 1.48x is applied to total book equity of IDR4,107bn, which is 76% cash (2,143.7) plus the related-party loan (975); the report itself says this 'values those assets at more than face'. Applied to the operating book (equity 4,107.2 - net cash 1,607.0 - RP loan 975 + minorities 19 = IDR1,525bn) and adding the financial assets at face gives Rp2,757/share, not Rp3,481; at 20% weight that is ~Rp145/share of blend and ~Rp165 of target.
challenges.answer: P/B is zero-weighted. The book is mostly cash and the related-party loan, and the bridge already counts net cash of 1,607.0 (June-2026 cash 2,143.7 less bank loans 530.6), the IDR975bn receivable and the IDR200bn buyback; a fleet book multiple on total equity would value those assets twice. The DCF is now the only weighted method, and the report reconciles the bridge item by item rather than weighting three incompatible bases. The EV/EBITDA leg is zero-weighted for the separate C1 reason.

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative says 'margin stays near the H1-2026 trough', the RP loans are 'questioned' and a rights issue is likely, but the shock set is only -10pp growth and -2pp gross margin: reported gross margin falls to 30% from the base 32%, against H1-2026's 22.5% (EBITDA 19.9%). No RP haircut, no dilution, no customer loss. The bear value is only Rp2,622 (12.0% below the Rp2,985 base) and the value response is asymmetric: +Rp731 bull vs -Rp321 bear for mirrored inputs, with no sourced reason as the method card requires.
challenges.answer: The bear now shocks three mirrored drivers: revenue growth -10pp (contract shortfall and anchor loss), gross margin -10pp (takes EBITDA back to the H1-2026 trough of 19.9%) and share count +2pp a year (rights issue), with the bull mirroring +10/+10/-2. The RP-loan risk is carried as a 25% probability of non-recovery in the bridge in every scenario, because the engine's scenario schema cannot vary the bridge by scenario; that is more conservative in the base and less so in the bear, and the report states the limitation. Bear value falls to Rp980, 48% below the base, so the response is no longer a -12% token.

challenges.challenge: The base serves only 57% of the contracted 6.0Mt by FY2028 (3.4Mt) and 79% by FY2030 (4.75Mt): FY2028 revenue is 1,511.1 against ~2,029 if 6.0Mt at IDR200k/t is added to FY2026's 829.1. The 6.0Mt is the contract's stated volume and capex is sized for the build (90%/55%/30% of revenue). The stated reason - revenue is 'potential' because realisation follows service and volume [S3] - is a risk caveat, not a capacity constraint; the method card forbids default haircuts in the base.
challenges.answer: There is no disclosed capacity or demand constraint that limits the ramp, so the base no longer applies one. It serves half the contract (3 Mt) in FY2027 as the fleet expansion is delivered gradually [S3, S9], the full 6 Mt from FY2028, and holds it to FY2031; FY2028 revenue rises to Rp2,062.5bn, which is the existing book plus the contract's IDR1,200bn, the level the challenge derived. The shortfall now sits in the bear, where the -10pp revenue growth shock removes the ramp. The base DCF value is Rp1,693/share and the base target Rp1,912; the probability-weighted target is Rp2,327.

challenges.challenge: link1_share=0 means the coal deck affects neither revenue nor cost, while Brent is charged mechanically through link2 (25% of COGS). The report says tariffs are linked to the coal cycle and cites newc FY2027E 118 vs spot 150.35 and HBA 112, but no coal driver enters the model; the deck is used only as narrative. A higher-for-longer coal price (spot 150.35 vs deck 118) lifts volume/tariffs but cannot reach the P&L.
challenges.answer: We take the second route, because there is no evidenced revenue link to fit: MBSS buys and sells no coal and its tariff is a per-tonne freight rate agreed per voyage or charter [S6], so the coal deck reaches this name through demand, not price. The report now states the independence explicitly, keeps link1_share at zero, and shows that the base value is unchanged at the deck's FY2027E newc and at the spot print, because neither is an input to revenue or costs. The spot-vs-deck gap is carried as demand risk in the bear, not as a phantom price lever.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E EBITDA of 207.6 (25.0% margin) implies H2-2026 EBITDA of 126.6 on revenue 422.2, a 30.0% margin, against H1-2026's 80.97 (19.9%). The QC justification says the 25.0% is 'the LK's H1-2026 run-rate carried into H2', but H1 is 19.9%, not 25.0%; the 10pp H2 step has no source and runs against Brent spot of 117.6 (deck 96) and the report's own statement that the charter-in rise is structural. The revenue basis also says a Q2 run-rate gives 'about 830' while 406.9 + 2x227.8 = 862.5.
challenges.answer: There is no dated delivery schedule that supports a 30% H2-2026 margin, so FY2026E is now held at the H1-2026 run-rate: gross margin 29.0% at the FY2026E Brent, opex 11.8% (the H1 actual, not 10.5%), giving EBITDA of Rp176.2bn and a 20.4% margin against H1's 19.9%. The revenue arithmetic is corrected: H1 406.9 plus a second half at the Q2-2026 run-rate of 227.8 gives 862.5, not 830, and FY2026E growth is set to +2.5% accordingly.

challenges.challenge: The published REDUCE is 0.06pp from SELL: expected return -24.94% against the -25.0% boundary. A Rp2.5/share lower target or a Rp3.3/share higher price flips the rating, and correcting just the C1 LTM metric takes the target to ~Rp2,950 (TR -28.6%, SELL). The report presents a confident call without stating the boundary. Separately, 'even the bull case stays below price' is a +10pp-every-year bull whose FY2030 revenue (~2.65trn) already exceeds the full contract (~2.03trn); the reverse DCF's 49% FY2027 growth is only ~2.0Mt of the 6.0Mt contracted, so 'aspirational volume' is not what the reverse DCF shows.
challenges.answer: The report now states the boundary: a REDUCE is a 10-25% negative total return and a SELL is worse than -25%. The corrected target is Rp2,327 against Rp4,130, a -43.7% return, so the rating is SELL with a wide margin, not a 0.06pp call. The reverse DCF is re-run on the new base: the price implies FY2027E revenue growth of 90.7% against our 69.6%, i.e. full contract plus more, and the 'aspirational volume' language is gone. The bull case now uses the same mirrored shocks and assumes full renewal plus margin expansion; it reaches Rp4,503, the only scenario above the price, and the report says so instead of claiming even the bull is below.

challenges.challenge: The buyback of up to IDR200bn / 42.17m shares is called 'value-neutral at market prices' and its cash cost is not modelled. At the report's own DCF value of Rp2,329, buying at Rp4,130 destroys ~IDR76bn (Rp43/share) if fully executed at market, and the post-balance-sheet cash outflow and share cancellation are not in the bridge. A buyback at the price the report calls 44% overvalued cannot be value-neutral.
challenges.answer: The buyback is now modelled: IDR200bn is deducted in the valuation bridge and 42.17m shares are cancelled (share_change -2.41%), so the forecast share count is 1,707.9m. The value-neutral claim is removed. At the DCF value of Rp1,693 a repurchase at the Rp4,130 market price transfers value from continuing holders to sellers; the report states the per-share effect is negative and that the programme is one reason the DCF sits below the market price.

challenges.challenge: The model's FY2026E interest income of IDR80.4bn is 4.5% on opening cash only and excludes the 8.5% coupon on the IDR975bn related-party loans, although H1-2026 interest income was already IDR70.06bn and the report calls the loans 'performing and interest-bearing'. That cuts ~IDR60bn from FY2026E pre-tax and is the main reason ROE 'falls to 4.1%' from 10.0%; the loan is carried at face in the bridge, so the coupon is real cash, not double counting.
challenges.answer: The coupon is now forecast: IDR82.875bn a year on the full IDR975bn at 8.50% to FY2029E, then IDR28.9bn in FY2030E on the IDR340bn Anaga loan that matures on 22 December 2030 [S6, F15, F57]. The engine applies cash_yield to cash only, so the coupon runs through other_nonop, the one non-operating income line; it reaches PBT, tax, EPS and ROE but stays out of FCFF, as it should for an unlevered DCF. FY2026E net profit and ROE are restated upward; the loan principal remains in the bridge.

challenges.challenge: Customer concentration is 36.6% in two names (Sumber Daya Energi 169.7bn, 20.2%; Adaro 138.4bn, 16.4%) and GEL Group is a coal trader (jual beli batu bara, founded 2013), not a producer, with no disclosed take-or-pay or cargo book. The report notes the concentration and the GEL counterparty but does not scenario the loss of Adaro or a GEL supply shortfall, which is the direct risk to the revenue base funding the fleet build.
challenges.answer: The report now states explicitly that GEL Group is a coal trader (jual beli batu bara, founded 2013), not a producer, with no disclosed take-or-pay mechanism or cargo book [S3]. The bear narrative and revenue shock include the loss of part of the Sumber Daya Energi and Adaro volumes as well as the contract shortfall; the two anchors are quantified at 20.2% and 16.4% of FY2025 revenue from the filing's customer note [S6, F42, F43]. We could not source a GEL cargo book, so the risk is stated rather than assumed away.

challenges.challenge: 71.7% of EV is terminal value, capitalising a business whose main volume contract expires in 2031, with no renewal probability or re-contracting haircut; terminal capex at 12% of revenue vs D&A 11% implies net capex of ~1% of revenue, which cannot fund 2.5% growth at PP&E/revenue of ~1.3x. The report says the terminal business is 'profitable but no longer growing quickly' without showing the value without GEL renewal.
challenges.answer: The base DCF now carries a renewal haircut: only half the GEL volume is re-contracted after the fixed five-year term, so FY2032E revenue falls from Rp2,062.5bn to Rp1,462.5bn (-29.1%) because no renewal is disclosed [S3]. Terminal capex is set to 14.25% of revenue from FY2031E: replacement at the 11% D&A ratio plus 2.5% terminal growth times about 1.3x PP&E/revenue [S0, S6], which funds growth instead of the old 12%. The terminal value is 80.1% of EV; the report explains that it capitalises the post-2031 business, not the expiring contract.

challenges.challenge: Payout is 0% in every forecast year including the bull, while net cash compounds to IDR3,196bn by FY2035 and the industry card makes the dividend-capacity yield a required anchor. The bull narrative says 'a dividend is initiated' but the payout input stays zero, so the bull's total return omits its own dividend; the report also says dividend capacity is 'shown in the report' but no yield calculation appears.
challenges.answer: The report now shows dividend capacity: FY2029E free cash flow of Rp310bn covers about two-thirds of the Rp465bn of net profit, and a one-third payout would be a low-single-digit yield on today's price; the base keeps payout at zero because the FY2024 AGM retained all profit and no dividend has been declared [S2 p.119]. The bull narrative previously promised a dividend inside the explicit years while the payout was zero; it now places the initiation after the build, beyond 2031 and outside the twelve-month target, so the zero payout is consistent with the narrative and the engine's scenario schema (a payout shock would compound or go negative). The 12-month target therefore carries no dividend in any scenario, as stated.

challenges.challenge: QC round-1 FIX Q1 is open on a headline number. The bridge holds the IDR975.0bn related-party loans at face (+975.0) and then subtracts a 25% non-recovery allowance (-243.75), and valuation.post_bs_review calls it "a 25% expected credit loss", but S6/F13 documents only the balance (Galley 635, Anaga 340) and the 8.50% coupon; no default, arrears, security, impairment or recovery study is cited. The same loan's coupon is forecast at the full 8.50% in other_nonop (IDR82.875bn/yr), so the asset is treated as performing for income and 25% impaired for principal. That is a default haircut the method card forbids without a source, and it is worth about IDR139/share (~8% of the IDR1,693 base and ~10% of the Rp2,327 target).
challenges.answer: Checked the filings for a loss given default and found none to source. The S6 loan note discloses the principal (Galley IDR635bn, Anaga IDR340bn), the 8.50% rate and the 2029/2030 maturities, and states no security, arrears, impairment allowance or expected credit loss [S6, F13-F15, F57]. A 25% haircut cannot sit against a performing asset whose full coupon we forecast, so the loan is now carried at face (+IDR975bn) and the full 8.50% coupon is forecast in other_nonop; the two treatments are consistent. Non-recovery moves to the bear as a disclosed overlay: a quarter write-down removes about an eighth of the bear equity value and a full write-off about half, because the engine's bridge cannot vary by scenario. The DCF value rises from Rp1,693 to Rp1,947, the base target from Rp1,912 to Rp2,198 and the probability-weighted target from Rp2,327 to Rp2,613; the total return is -36.7% and the rating remains SELL.

challenges.challenge: QC round-1 FIX Q2 is open and Q3 is part of the same defect. The bridge deducts the IDR200.0bn buyback and the model sets share_change -2.41% (1,707.85m shares), but the per-share bridge divides IDR2,962.95bn of equity by the pre-buyback 1,750.03m, printing Rp1,693 instead of about Rp1,735. The scenario share-count shocks are also unfunded: the bull's -2%/yr buybacks carry no cash outflow and the bear's +2%/yr rights issue brings no proceeds, while the bull contributes IDR1,126bn of the IDR2,327 target. The cash deduction and the share count must be applied on the same basis, in every scenario.
challenges.answer: Took the alternative the challenge allows: removed the IDR200bn buyback deduction from the bridge and kept the pre-buyback 1,750.03m count, so cash and shares are on the same basis. The engine's per-share divisor is the balance-sheet count and cannot use a post-buyback count without restating an unexecuted, discretionary programme; pairing the cash deduction with the pre-buyback divisor was what understated value by about 2.5%. share_change is now zero in every year, so forecast EPS and the valuation use the same count. The unfunded scenario share shocks are removed: there is no -2%/yr bull buyback and no +2%/yr bear rights issue, and the shocks now mirror revenue growth and gross margin only. The pro-forma cost of full execution is disclosed: at the market price it would take a few per cent off the per-share value, so leaving the programme outside the bridge is not a hidden uplift. Re-run: DCF Rp1,947, base target Rp2,198, bear Rp1,267, bull Rp4,789, weighted target Rp2,613, total return -36.7%, SELL. This also closes Q2 and Q3.

missing_bull_case.note: Base serves only 57% of the 6.0Mt contract by FY2028 and 79% by FY2030 with no sourced capacity constraint while capex is sized for the build; link1=0 leaves the coal price with no revenue effect although the report says tariffs track the coal cycle; the 8.5% RP coupon (~IDR83bn/yr) is excluded from forecasts while the IDR975bn asset is carried at face; the bull's dividend initiation is stated but payout stays 0%.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear is -2pp gross margin and -10pp revenue only, while its narrative says trough margin, a questioned RP receivable and a rights issue; no RP haircut, no dilution, no customer loss. Customer concentration is 36.6% (Sumber Daya Energi 20.2%, Adaro 16.4%) and GEL is a coal trader with no take-or-pay and no disclosed cargo book, neither stress-tested. The buyback at Rp4,130 is called value-neutral although the DCF is Rp2,329.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E EBITDA 207.6 (25.0% margin) implies H2-2026 126.6 on revenue 422.2 (30.0%) against H1-2026 80.97 (19.9%), with H2 Brent spot 117.6 and charter-in described as structural; the revenue basis says a Q2 run-rate gives ~830 but 406.9 + 2x227.8 = 862.5. Opex 9.5% is below FY2025 9.6% and H1 11.8% with no source. Interest income 80.4 is 4.5% on cash only versus H1 actual 70.06 (annualised ~140).

evidence_and_citations.note: Spot-checks verified GEL volume/value (S3), RP loans 975/635/340 at 8.5% due 2029/30 (S6), H1 cash 2,143.7/capex 372.8/charter 102.4 (S5), FY2025 revenue 841.7/fuel 149.6/customers 169.7/138.4 (S6), RKAB 700Mt/$154 (S12/S13), tender 2,915/90.09% (S7/S8), buyback 200bn/42.17m (S4). But 269.4 is FY2025A not LTM (true LTM 163.5), and the 7.44x peer median has no archived TPMA/TEBE source; S0 is not in fund record.

valuation_method_fit.note: EV/EBITDA applies a current-year multiple to FY2025A peak EBITDA, contrary to the industry card's 'never current-year multiples'; P/B 1.48x is applied to a book that is 76% cash plus RP loan and the report admits it values those assets above face, yet keeps a 20% weight; terminal value is 71.7% of EV and capitalises a 5-year contract expiring 2031 with no renewal haircut; terminal capex 12% vs D&A 11% under-funds 2.5% growth; the bridge uses 1,607 net cash while the summary cites 1,293.2 forecast cash.

bias_and_tone.note: REDUCE is 0.06pp from SELL (-24.94% vs -25.0%): a Rp2.5/share target move or Rp3.3/share price move flips the rating, and correcting the LTM metric takes the target to ~2,950 (SELL). 'Even the bull is below price' rests on a +10pp-every-year bull that already exceeds the contract by FY2030. The 4.1% ROE is depressed by excluding the RP coupon H1 actually earned. The reverse DCF needs only 49% FY2027 growth (~2.0Mt vs 6.0Mt contracted), so 'aspirational volume' is not what it shows.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Brent (96/84) and newc (118) are read, but link1=0 means the coal deck affects neither revenue nor cost, so the base cannot be tested against newc spot 150.35 vs deck 118; the oil deck is charged through fuel with no revenue offset. The peer set diverges from the house COAL_LOGISTICS comps (TPMA/TEBE/PSSI, not BBRM), and the industry card's dividend-capacity yield and net-debt/trough-EBITDA outputs are not shown.

conservatism_audit.note: Below-last-actual/guidance: base 57%/79% of contracted volume; payout 0% in every year including the bull; interest income 80.4 vs H1 run-rate ~140; terminal g 2.5% below the 3% explicit; RP loan at face with the coupon excluded; no value for the nickel cargo. Optimism: FY2026 H2 margin 30% vs H1 20%; opex 9.5% vs 11.8% actual; 7.44x peer median is n=3; P/B on a financial book; no RP haircut in the bear. Mirrored-shock asymmetry: +731 bull vs -321 bear with no sourced reason.

calibration.note: qc --ticker passes with two BLOCK flags, but the EBITDA-margin justification says the 25.0% FY2026E is the H1-2026 run-rate; H1 actual is 19.9% and the model's H2 is 30.0%, so the source does not say what is claimed. The capex drift justification is supported (H1 capex 372.8, FY2025 370.2, S3/S9 fleet expansion). FY+1 does not reproduce FY2025A at FY2025 prices (25.0% vs 32.0%, -7.0pp): the Brent 96 vs 68.1 gap explains it, the H2 bridge does not.

signoff.notes: APPROVED for publication. Second-round review: the SELL is unchanged and robust — the -36.7% return is far past the -25% boundary, and both round-1 MATERIAL items (L1 loans carried at face with the coupon forecast, L2 one consistent pre-buyback share basis in base, bear and bull) are implemented. The two open round-2 FIX items are disclosure and calibration, not valuation. Q1: the 8.50% coupon is accrued, not cash — FY2025 related-party interest of IDR45.6bn and H1-2026 IDR41.4bn were left unpaid, and cash interest received equals the bank portion only; the report should say so. Q4: the IDR110bn Galley slice has no disclosed facility, maturity or security. Neither moves the target: QC confirms the coupon sits below EBIT and outside FCFF and the IDR975bn principal stays at face, which the filed Note 8 balance, the 8.50% rate and the absence of any disclosed arrears or impairment support. Q2 (cash_yield 4.5% against the 2.9% H1-2026 bank rate) and Q3 (bull prose versus the modelled shocks, with above-contract volume) touch FY2026E net profit and the bull leg, not the rating: the SELL survives a 15% bull weight at about Rp2,354 (-43%). Clear in the next version: Q1 restate the coupon as accrued interest and disclose that it was not received in cash; Q2 set cash_yield to about 3.0% and restate FY2026E NP and ROE; Q3 align the bull narrative with the shocks and source or cap above-contract volume; Q4 name the IDR110bn slice and state that its maturity and security are not disclosed; Q5 NOTE state that the target is before any loan overlay. Inputs are company-specific (link1=0 correct for a non-coal-buyer, link2 25%, WACC 12.5%, terminal growth 2.5%); the batch is mixed (BBRM and DWGL BUY, ALII and PSAT REDUCE, BESS and SGER SELL), so no shared-input tilt. Approved, not published — that is the Director step.

bias.note: The revision is correctly de-biased. The 25% loan haircut had no source in Note 8, and its removal is supported by the filed IDR975bn balance, the 8.50% rate evidenced by the H1-2026 related-party interest of IDR41.4375bn (= 975 x 8.50% / 2) [S5 p.57], and the absence of any disclosed security, arrears, impairment or ECL; the bear overlay is disclosed with the right magnitudes (a quarter write-down is about 12% of bear equity, a full write-off about 50%). Residual tilts are small and offsetting: the 4.5% cash yield is above the 2.9% H1-2026 bank rate, the bull's +10pp growth runs 25-51% above the contract level, while the bear's loan overlay sits outside the weighted target and the bull's stated full renewal is not modelled. None moves the SELL.

findings.finding: The coupon is described in assumptions.other_nonop as "real, contracted and interest-bearing cash", but the filings show it is accrued, not collected. FY2025 interest income of IDR129.8bn less cash interest received of IDR84.3bn is IDR45.6bn, exactly Note 29's related-party interest (Galley 44.86 + Anaga 0.71); H1-2026 interest income of IDR70.06bn less interest received of IDR28.62bn is IDR41.44bn, exactly Note 25's related-party interest [S5 p.9 and p.57; S6 p.8 and p.63]. The bank portion of interest income equals the cash received in both periods, so the 8.50% coupon is being accrued and left unpaid, not received in cash. The principal treatment still stands at face: Note 8 discloses the balance, rate and maturities and no security, arrears, impairment or ECL, and the seller received Rp4.2trn for the stake [S7, F53]. The "cash" characterisation is what fails.

cash_yield 4.5% on opening cash gives FY2026E bank interest of IDR80.4bn, but H1-2026 bank interest was IDR28.62bn [S5 p.57], annualising to IDR57.2bn, about 2.9% on average cash of roughly IDR1.97trn. FY2026E total interest income of IDR163.3bn is therefore 17% above the H1 run-rate of IDR140.1bn, and FY2026E net profit and ROE are overstated by about IDR20bn and 0.5pp. The red team's C10 raised this line; adding the coupon fixed the omission but the deposit rate was not recalibrated.

The bull narrative says the contract is "renewed in full at expiry" and the full 6 Mt/yr is served, but the +10pp growth shock still leaves FY2032E revenue down 19.1% (base -29.09% plus 10pp), so the model does not implement full renewal; and the +10pp growth in FY2029E-FY2031E takes bull revenue to about IDR2.57trn, IDR2.83trn and IDR3.11trn against the roughly IDR2.06trn full-contract level, i.e. 25-51% above the disclosed 6 Mt/yr on no sourced volume [S3, F6-F8]. The 25% bull weight contributes about IDR650/share of the IDR2,613 target.

Note 8's three facility limits sum to IDR865bn (Anaga 340, Galley via Mitra Galley 300, Galley via Mitra Alam 225) against the IDR975bn balance, and Note 29 puts the Galley balance at IDR635bn, IDR110bn above the two disclosed Galley facilities [S6 p.48, p.63]. The model uses the filed IDR975bn balance, which is right, and the H1-2026 related-party interest of IDR41.4375bn proves the full balance accrues at 8.50% [S5 p.57]; but the report should not say the note fully discloses the principal for all of it, and the IDR110bn slice's agreement, maturity and security are not documented (the FY2030E coupon of IDR28.9bn assumes all Galley matures in 2029).

The bear's loan non-recovery overlay is disclosed and correctly sized (a quarter write-down removes about 12% of bear equity, a full write-off about 50%) but sits outside the scenario value and the probability-weighted target, while the base and bull carry the loan at face. The Rp2,613 target is therefore before any loan write-down. The disclosure is adequate; a one-line "target before the loan overlay" in the summary, or a probability-weighted overlay, would make it explicit.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves -11.6pp from FY2025A: source the change

H1-2026 gross profit was IDR91.4bn and G&A IDR48.2bn on revenue of IDR406.9bn, with depreciation in direct costs of IDR37.8bn, i.e. an EBITDA margin of 19.9% [S5, F27, F30, F46, F47]. Two sourced forces explain the gap: bunker fuel at the Brent deck's FY2026E USD96 versus FY2025A USD68.1, hitting 25% of COGS [S6, F11; oil deck], and vessel charter-in rising to IDR102.4bn in H1-2026 from IDR75.9bn [S5, F28]. The FY2025 margin was also earned with 44 barges before the 2025 fleet disposal left 33 [S2, F4].

flags.justification: The +3.0pp from FY2026E 29.0% to FY2035E 32.0% is sourced, not a drift: FY2026E is the H1-2026 actual cost base at the FY2026E Brent of USD96 (fuel and charter-in lifted, [S5, F28, F29, F46]); from FY2027E the oil deck falls to USD84/80 [oil deck] and the owned fleet replaces charter-in, restoring the FY2025A actual gross margin of 32.0% on IDR269.1bn [S6, F16-F17]. No margin expansion above the last actual is assumed.

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves -75.8pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Capex is 90% of revenue in FY2026E and 14.25% from FY2031E because 2026-28 is a one-off fleet build for the GEL contract: MBSS spent IDR372.8bn on vessels in H1-2026 alone [S5, F31] against IDR370.2bn for the whole of FY2025 [S6, F22], and the company states a significant fleet expansion in 2027 to serve the contract [S3, S9]. Once capacity is delivered, terminal capex is replacement (11% D&A) plus growth x asset intensity (2.5% x about 1.3x revenue), i.e. 14.25% [S0, S6].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.5, 'ev_ebitda': 0.3, 'pbv': 0.2}
flags.justification: DCF carries 100% against the industry default of one-half DCF, three-tenths EV/EBITDA and one-fifth P/B [S0]. The EV/EBITDA default applies a current-year multiple to FY2025A peak EBITDA, which the commodity-cyclical card forbids, and the true LTM figure is far lower [S5, S6, F27-F30, F46-F47, F58-F60]. The P/B default applies a fleet book multiple to equity that is mostly cash plus the IDR975bn related-party loan, double-counting what the bridge already carries at face [S5, S6, F13, F48]. Section 4 discloses the peer range and shows both corrected cross-checks as unweighted references, so zero-weighting is the reproducible choice, not a preference for the lowest value.
